For those unaware of how the All-MLB team gets selected, this is the description from the press release: Fans and panelists will vote for their choices at catcher, first base, second base, third base, shortstop, three outfielders (without regard for left/center/right) and designated hit
item.content:encoded:
Two Mets are on the ballot for the 2026 'All-MLB' team, Juan Soto and Nolan McLean. Voting opens today and runs through Friday, October 9. The team will be announced at the MLB Awards on November 11 in Las Vegas. For those unaware of how the All-MLB team gets selected, this is the description from the press release:
Fans and panelists will vote for their choices at catcher, first base, second base, third base, shortstop, three outfielders (without regard for left/center/right) and designated hitter, along with five starting pitchers and two relief pitchers on both the first and second teams. All choices will be based on the 2026 regular season, without regard for American League or National League affiliation.
McLean, a Rookie of the Year contender, put up 3.0 bWAR in his first full season alongside a 3.16 ERA, 128 ERA+, 194 strikeouts in 179 and two-thirds innings, while making 31 starts. Soto, who missed 51 games due to injury, also put up 3.0 bWAR while hitting .275/.393/.515 with 27 home runs and a 154 OPS+.
Other outfield selections include Pete Crow-Armstrong, Mike Trout, James Wood, and Byron Buxton. Other starting pitcher nominees include Sandy Alcantara, Jacob deGrom, Zack Wheeler, and Tarik Skubal.
The full list of nominees can be found here, and you can vote here.

item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Orioles didn't have a great 2026 season, but the presence of Pete Alonso provided a spark worth getting excited about moving forward.
He led the American League in home runs and put up a 4.9 bWAR season, the best season he's had since his 2019 rookie year with the New York Mets. But Alonso has made MLB history with a different season during his Mets tenure.
Sarah Langs shared that Alonso is the first hitter in MLB history since 1920 to lead the American League and the National League in RBIs, as he led the NL in RBIs in 2022 and the AL in 2026.
Pete Alonso made MLB history that surprisingly hasn't happened before
"Pete Alonso led the AL in RBI. He led the NL (and tied for the MLB lead) in 2022. He's the first player to have a season leading each league in RBI in his career (RBI since 1920)," Langs shared.
In 2026 with the Orioles, Alonso has 113 RBIs, which is the most in the American League, although it's not the most in Major League Baseball.
Back in 2022, Alonso had 131 RBIs, the most in the NL and all of MLB that season. Combined with his 2026 production, Alonso has become the first player to finish a season as the league leader in the AL and NL in RBIs.
This is an unexpected MLB record for Alonso, as it's a bit surprising that no other player was ever able to accomplish this fairly straightforward feat.
While players weren't changing teams back then as much as they do now, it's still unexpected that this has never happened before.
But this is still a very impressive feat for Alonso, as he's now the only player to lead both the AL and NL in RBIs in a single season.
He's also led the AL and NL in home runs, hitting 53 homers in his rookie season to lead all of MLB, and hitting 43 homers in 2026 to lead the AL, two behind Pete Crow-Armstrong and Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead.
This statistic highlights how great Alonso has been for the Orioles, as the new first baseman has become a massive piece of the Orioles' franchise and should be the focal point moving forward for a new era of Orioles baseball.

item.title: [MLB.com] Fresh off facial fractures, Bregman mashes 2 homers in 2nd game back
item.dc:creator: Jordan Bastian
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG – Even without any postseason implications on the line on Sunday, Alex Bregman told Cubs manager Craig Counsell that he wanted to be in the starting lineup. The third baseman felt it was important for him to get more at-bats ahead of the playoffs. And if there were any lingering questions about how Bregman was seeing the ball just a week removed from the fluke foul ball that resulted in multiple fractures in his left cheek, he offered an emphatic answer against the Red Sox. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – Even without any postseason implications on the line on Sunday, Alex Bregman told Cubs manager Craig Counsell that he wanted to be in the starting lineup. The third baseman felt it was important for him to get more at-bats ahead of the playoffs.
And if there were any lingering questions about how Bregman was seeing the ball just a week removed from the fluke foul ball that resulted in multiple fractures in his left cheek, he offered an emphatic answer against the Red Sox. In only his second game back in the lineup, Bregman belted a pair of no-doubt homers in his first two at-bats at Tropicana Field.
Following two games on Friday at Fenway Park, where strong winds related to the Nor’easter hitting the region did a number on Chicago’s offense, the move to the neutral site gave the lineup a chance to hit reset. That was especially important for Bregman, who went 0-for-4 in his first game back in the opener of Friday’s twin bill.
Late Saturday night, Bregman went over video with Ben Martin, an assistant director of Major League development for the Cubs, at the team’s hotel. They found some issues with Bregman’s posture in his stance during Friday’s at-bats and went to work on correcting the issue. And on Sunday afternoon, Counsell received a text message from the third baseman.
“It just said, ‘LFG,’” Counsell said with a smirk. “I knew what it meant – I didn’t know what he was referring to. I thought he was referring to a football game or something like that. But he was like, ‘I found it and I’m ready. I feel good.’ And yeah, he did. He felt good. He was right.”
Bregman cracked a smile when asked about the text.
“[We were] trying to figure out what felt a little weird the first game back,” Bregman said. “I was kind of looking uphill and kind of [leaning] back. So I kind of got a little bit more into it, into a little bit more of an attacking posture today. It felt better.”
That is great news ahead of the upcoming National League Wild Card Series against the Padres.
“I’m not surprised that he’s performing when he’s back on the field,” Counsell said. “I’m surprised that he’s back on the field. Being back on the field is what I think we should all appreciate and admire.”
The only question right now is whether Counsell will put Bregman back at third base in the postseason, or keep him slotted in as the designated hitter for now. Bregman has been the DH in his first two games back in the fold, and Counsell hinted at staying in that mode as a way to minimize the risk of a setback.
Bregman took ground balls in a workout at Tropicana Field on Saturday’s off-day and will do so again during Monday’s workout at Petco Park in San Diego. Even so, Counsell is taking things day by day when it comes to weighing putting him back in the field.
“We’ll just kind of see how he feels every day,” Counsell said. “I think he’s improving every day, but he’s got multiple face fractures, and it’s been [a week]. So we’ll just see how he feels. One thing I’m thinking about is the risk of more exposure. I think his at-bats are the most important thing that we can get.”
Bregman said he is willing to do whatever Counsell asks of him.
“I want to play third, but I’ll do whatever it takes,” Bregman said.
Bregman went deep in the first and third inning – off a first-pitch sinker and then an 0-1 sweeper – and sent both pitches crashing into the left-field stands. Those were the 27th and 28th homers of the year for Bregman, who has been one of baseball’s best hitters in the second half. Entering the final game of the regular season, only Pete Crow-Armstrong (4.7), Fernando Tatis Jr. (3.7) and Elly De La Cruz (3.6) had a higher WAR (via FanGraphs) than Bregman (3.3) since the All-Star break.
Bregman added a single in the fifth inning, drew a walk in the seventh and added an RBI double in the ninth. When he reached base after those plate appearances, Bregman switched out one helmet (with an extended left earflap) for another that had a longer flap on each side to offer more protection.
“I felt like I was in a football helmet out there,” Bregman quipped.
Bregman was waiting on deck on Sept. 20 in Cincinnati when he was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch. Prior to that game, the Cubs’ third baseman had hit .298 with 19 homers, 18 doubles, 53 RBIs and a 1.000 OPS in his previous 60 games. His season OPS climbed to .801 from .670 in that span.
Beyond the homers, Bregman ended the year slashing .265/.355/.464 with 33 doubles, 76 walks, 92 runs scored, 93 RBIs and an .819 OPS in 155 games for the North Siders.
“The last two months of the season, I feel like that’s who I am as a player,” Bregman said. “I’m proud to know that no matter how big of a hole that I dug myself, I could find my way back out.”

item.dc:creator: Jordan Bastian
item.description: ST. El antesalista consideraba importante sumar más turnos al bate de cara a los playoffs. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG -- Incluso sin nada en juego en cuanto a la postemporada el domingo, Alex Bregman le dijo al manager de los Cachorros, Craig Counsell, que quería estar en la alineación titular. El antesalista consideraba importante sumar más turnos al bate de cara a los playoffs.
Y si quedaba alguna duda sobre cómo Bregman estaba viendo la pelota apenas una semana después del inusual foul que le provocó múltiples fracturas en la mejilla izquierda, ofreció una respuesta contundente contra los Medias Rojas. Apenas en su segundo juego de regreso a la alineación, Bregman disparó dos contundentes jonrones en sus primeros dos turnos al bate en el Tropicana Field.
Después de disputar dos juegos el viernes en el Fenway Park, donde los fuertes vientos relacionados con la tormenta del nordeste que azotaba la región afectaron considerablemente a la ofensiva de Chicago, el traslado a una sede neutral le dio a la alineación la oportunidad de empezar de cero. Eso era especialmente importante para Bregman, quien se fue de 4-0 en su primer partido de regreso, en el primer encuentro de la doble cartelera del viernes.
“Sentí como si no hubiera jugado en varios días, pero mi rostro estaba bien”, dijo Bregman el viernes. “Vi bien la pelota. Así que espero poder aprovechar esos turnos y volver a sentirme como me sentía antes”.
Si lo ocurrido el domingo sirve como indicio, el swing de Bregman luce en buena forma de cara a la próxima Serie del Comodín de la Liga Nacional contra los Padres.
La única interrogante en estos momentos es si Counsell volverá a colocar a Bregman en la tercera base durante la postemporada o si, por ahora, lo mantendrá como bateador designado. Bregman ha sido el BD en sus primeros dos juegos de regreso, y Counsell dio indicios de que podría mantenerlo en ese rol como una manera de reducir el riesgo de un contratiempo.
Bregman tomó rodados durante una práctica en el Tropicana Field en el día libre del sábado, pero Counsell está evaluando la situación día a día a la hora de considerar su regreso a la defensa.
“Tenemos que tomar una decisión al respecto, sin duda”, dijo Counsell. “Simplemente veremos cómo se siente cada día. Creo que mejora día tras día, pero tiene múltiples fracturas faciales y ha pasado [una semana]. Así que veremos cómo se siente. Una de las cosas en las que estoy pensando es el riesgo de exponerlo más.
“Creo que sus turnos al bate son lo más importante que podemos obtener. Entonces, ¿vale la pena esa exposición? ¿Nos hace realmente mucho mejores a costa de poner en riesgo esos turnos? Eso es lo que tenemos que considerar. Y, por supuesto, también la salud y el bienestar del jugador”.
Bregman conectó cuadrangulares en el primer y tercer innings, primero ante un sinker en el primer pitcheo y luego frente a un sweeper con cuenta de 0-1, enviando ambos lanzamientos a las gradas del jardín izquierdo. Fueron los vuelacercas 27 y 28 del año para Bregman, quien ha sido uno de los mejores bateadores del béisbol en la segunda mitad de la temporada. Antes del último juego de la campaña regular, sólo Pete Crow-Armstrong (4.7), los dominicanos Fernando Tatis Jr. (3.7) y Elly De La Cruz (3.6) tenían un WAR más alto, según FanGraphs, que Bregman (3.3) desde la pausa del Juego de Estrellas.
Bregman agregó un sencillo en el quinto episodio, negoció un boleto en el séptimo y sumó un doble productor en el noveno. Cuando llegó a base después de esos turnos, Bregman cambió un casco, que tenía una extensión sobre la oreja izquierda, por otro con una protección más larga a cada lado para brindarle mayor seguridad.
Bregman se encontraba en el círculo de espera el 20 de septiembre en Cincinnati cuando recibió en el rostro una pelota de foul bateada por Michael Busch. Antes de ese juego, el antesalista de los Cachorros había bateado .298 con 19 jonrones, 18 dobles, 53 carreras impulsadas y OPS de 1.000 en sus 60 encuentros anteriores. Durante ese período, su OPS de la temporada subió de .670 a .801.
“Estoy entusiasmado por la postemporada. Tengo muchas ganas de que llegue”, dijo Bregman el viernes. “Siento que hoy se trataba de tomar algunos turnos al bate y volver a entrar en ritmo. Quería asegurarme de no estar pensando en nada relacionado con mi rostro y de que lo único que pasara por mi mente fuera lo mismo en lo que normalmente pienso cuando juego béisbol. Y así fue. No pensé en eso ni una sola vez”.

item.title: [LancasterOnline] Alex Bregman's huge day at the plate in relocated season finale powers Cubs to 6-2 win over Red Sox

item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Alex Bregman went 4 for 4 with two home runs and four RBIs in his second game back from a frightening injury, and the Chicago Cubs beat the Boston Red Sox 6-2 on Sunday in a regular-season finale that was relocated to Tropicana Field.
Chicago is the No. 5 seed in the National League playoffs and will play a best-of-three Wild Card Series at fourth-seeded San Diego beginning Tuesday night.
Boston is the No. 5 seed in the American League playoffs and will travel to New York to open its Wild Card Series the same night against the rival Yankees.
Major League Baseball moved the Cubs-Red Sox season finale to Florida because of a weekend nor’easter that was expected to batter the Boston area into Monday. Ahead of the storm, the Red Sox swept a doubleheader from the Cubs on Friday at Fenway Park.
Bregman went 0 for 4 with a strikeout at designated hitter in the opener — five days after sustaining facial fractures when he was struck in the face by a foul ball while standing in the on-deck circle.
The three-time All-Star third baseman, who played for Boston last year, was the DH again Sunday and fared much better at the plate in his final postseason tuneup. In addition to finishing a triple shy of the cycle, he drew a walk and scored three times.
With the NL MVP award virtually locked up, Pete Crow-Armstrong singled to open the game before Cubs manager Craig Counsell immediately removed him for pinch-runner Tyrone Taylor. Bregman launched the next pitch from Tanner Houck (0-1) into the left-field seats.
Adley Rutschman hit a solo homer off Chicago starter Shota Imanaga, who was lifted after one inning with postseason seeding already decided.
Braxton Garrett (1-1) pitched five strong innings in relief for his first win since May 29, 2024. Colin Rea earned his second save.
Played at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays, the game drew 20,411 fans who had less than 48 hours’ notice to purchase tickets.
Chicago finished 89-73, three games shy of its 92-70 mark in 2025.
Boston, which was 89-73 in 2025, ended the season 87-75. The Red Sox fired manager Alex Cora following a 10-17 start and replaced him with Chad Tracy.
Under Tracy, Boston became the first team to qualify for the postseason after dropping as many as 44 of its initial 75 games.

item.title: [Bleed Cubbie Blue] Cubs 6, Red Sox 2: Alex Bregman is more than ready for the postseason
item.dc:creator: Al Yellon
item.description: Last Sunday, Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch in Cincinnati. He suffered facial fractures and missed three games. Bregman came back Friday as the DH and Sunday, just a bit over exactly one week since that accident, he hit two home runs and also singled, doubled and walked. His 4-for-4 afternoon led the Cubs to a 4-2 Game 162 win over the Red Sox, a game played at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida. Bregman didn’t waste any time Sunday, either.
item.content:encoded:
Last Sunday, Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch in Cincinnati. He suffered facial fractures and missed three games.
Bregman came back Friday as the DH and Sunday, just a bit over exactly one week since that accident, he hit two home runs and also singled, doubled and walked. His 4-for-4 afternoon led the Cubs to a 4-2 Game 162 win over the Red Sox, a game played at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
Bregman didn’t waste any time Sunday, either. Pete Crow-Armstrong led off the game with a single and then departed for pinch-runner Tyrone Taylor.
That was great to see. Bregman seemed totally locked in from the moment he stepped into the batter’s box. And that ball was crushed! [VIDEO].
Shōta Imanaga started for the Cubs and threw just the first inning, allowing a home run to Adley Rutschman. That was the 35th homer off Imanaga this year, second-most in MLB this year to Aaron Nola’s 37. Imanaga threw only 12 pitches in this game, which theoretically leaves him available to pitch in the Wild Card Series, maybe Thursday or perhaps even Wednesday. Apart from the homer, Imanaga struck out the other three hitters he faced.
Braxton Garrett, who the Cubs acquired from the Marlins at the trade deadline for minor leaguers Jonathon Long and Jace Beck and who’d been at Triple-A Iowa since, was recalled for this game and went into the game as the “bulk guy” and threw very well. Garrett threw five innings and allowed four hits and a run, though he did issue three walks. He threw 70 pitches and will be in the mix for a starting rotation spot next year.
Bregman drove in all four Cubs runs in this game and finishes with 93 RBI on the season. It’s so good to see him productive after that freak injury. Even if he is limited to DH duty for the Wild Card Series, as noted on the Marquee broadcast, he’s been the Cubs’ second-best hitter (behind PCA) all year and they are going to need that hitting. I noticed that Bregman was wearing a double-flap helmet on the basepaths, though as you can see, not when he hit the home runs.
BCB’s JohnW53 has this fact about Bregman’s two-homer afternoon:
Today’s game was Alex Bregman’s fifth of the season with multiple home runs. Pete Crow-Armstrong has seven such games; Dansby Swanson, three; and Michael Conforto, one, for a total of 16.
The Cubs had a team-record 20 such games last year. They had 19 in 2019, 18 in 1998 and 2004, and 17 in 1930 and 1958. They also had 16 in 2021.
Going into today, the Astros had 16 this year, second to the Rockies’ 18. The Padres had 15.
The Cubs flashed some glove while Garrett was in the game. Here’s a nice stop by Matt Shaw in the fifth [VIDEO].
Jacob Webb succeeded Garrett in the seventh inning and retired all three hitters he faced on just 10 pitches. I don’t think I have to tell you how important it would be if Webb could recover the form that got him 24 straight scoreless appearances before the big meltdown he had at the end of August in Seattle and Arizona.
Colin Rea entered to throw the eighth inning and also retired the Red Sox in order, on just six pitches.
The Cubs then put the game away with a three-run ninth. Miguel Amaya led off with a single and went to third on a single by Taylor. That brought up Bregman, and he came through yet again with this RBI double [VIDEO].
Fact about Bregman’s game from John:
Bregman is just the sixth Cub to hit multiple homers and also have at least one double, one single and one walk. He is the first to do so on the road.
Pete Crow-Armstrong did it in on Aug. 17 in the Cubs’ 10-inning, 7-5 win at home over the White Sox, with his second homer walking it off.
The four others:
Hank Sauer: May 2, 1954, in an 18-10, eight-inning loss to the Pirates
Ryne Sandberg: Aug. 10, 1989, in a 16-13 loss to the Phillies
Corey Patterson: Sept. 7, 2004, in a 7-6, 12-inning loss to the Expos
Chris Coghlan: Sept. 20, 2014, in an 8-7 win over the Dodgers
All had two homers, one double, one single and one walk.
Taylor stopped at third on Bregman’s double, but he then scored on this sac fly by Gabriel Arias [VIDEO].
As mentioned on the Marquee broadcast, Arias is a very good bench player. He can play all infield positions and his bat plays well enough, a really useful guy to have around. That made it 5-2. Ian Happ then struck out, but Michael Conforto doubled, scoring Bregman to give the Cubs a four-run lead [VIDEO].
Rea remained in the game in the ninth to finish up, and he recorded his second save. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
In other postseason-related news, the Phillies won Sunday and so they take the final wild card spot and will face the Braves in Atlanta in another Wild Card Series beginning Tuesday. The Rangers lost to the Twins, which clinched the A.L. West title for the Astros (who are leading the A’s late and likely will finish 81-81). Houston will host the White Sox in a Wild Card Series starting Tuesday.
One more game note from John:
The Cubs’ six runs made their final total 850, their fourth most in the Modern Era, which began in 1901. They scored 998 in 1930, 982 in 1929 and 855 in 2008. They played 156 games in the first two seasons and 161 in the last.
And for whatever it’s worth, the win gave the Cubs an 89-73 record to the Red Sox’ 87-75. That means that if, somehow, those two clubs meet in the World Series, the Cubs would have home field. The Cubs have the better record over four of the six American League postseason teams; only the Rays and Yankees are better.
So the Cubs will now head to San Diego to begin their own Wild Card Series against the Padres Tuesday evening. I’ll have lots to say about that over the next couple of days here, of course. Michael King has been announced as the Padres starter, but no Cubs starter has yet been named. It could be Matthew Boyd, who’d be going on normal rest, as he last pitched on Thursday against the Marlins at Wrigley Field.
Game time Tuesday is late, so get rested up! 9 p.m. CT, with the game on NBC Sports Network (cable) and streaming on Peacock.
Go Cubs!

item.title: [FanSided] Ronald Acuña Jr. quietly just gave baseball another reason to fear the Braves
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: At some point, you’ve probably heard the one about the guy who walks into a doctor’s office, or the horse who walks into a bar. In the case of Atlanta Braves superstar outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr., his story involves the man who walks into the batter’s box, subtly changes his stance and catches fire ahead of the playoffs. item.content:encoded:
At some point, you’ve probably heard the one about the guy who walks into a doctor’s office, or the horse who walks into a bar. In the case of Atlanta Braves superstar outfielder Ronald Acuña Jr., his story involves the man who walks into the batter’s box, subtly changes his stance and catches fire ahead of the playoffs.
As Major League Baseball’s Mark Bowman recently pointed out, the 2023 NL MVP made a slight tweak to his hitting approach late last month. Mired in a prolonged slump following two hamstring strains, Acuña Jr. did not play in an Aug. 27 win over the eventual NL West champion Dodgers.
Later that night, Acuña Jr. told Braves assistant coach Eddie Pérez he wanted to take early batting practice the next day. During said session, the five-time All-Star closed his stance and, according to Bowman, "backed off the plate a couple of inches [and] separated his feet another few inches.”
The results? Let’s just say the rest of Major League Baseball should be on high alert.
How Atlanta Braves superstar Ronald Acuña Jr. changed his stance and turned his season around
Entering play Sunday, Acuña Jr. is hitting .337 with seven home runs, 20 RBI and a .997 OPS in 112 plate appearances since returning to the lineup on Aug. 28. His batting average has skyrocketed from .235 to .255, and his OPS went from .748 to .796 in less than a month.
If you extrapolate those stats over a full season, Acuña Jr. would finish with 44 home runs, 37 doubles and 125 RBI. Here’s where things get especially interesting: Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez is considered the consensus AL MVP favorite, and he woke up Sunday hitting .316 with 42 home runs, 105 RBI and a 1.036 OPS.
But wait, you say. Acuña Jr. plays in the National League, so how would those numbers compare to Cubs star outfielder and MVP shoo-in Pete Crow-Armstrong? Great question. Crow-Armstrong entered Sunday hitting .278 with 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 31 doubles, 41 steals and a .941 OPS. In that case, we’re not sure whether PCA would be running away with the NL MVP.
“When he is healthy and he gets on one of these streaks, he’s one of the best players in baseball,” said Ozzie Albies, who has played with Acuña since the latter’s 2018 debut. “There's nothing else to say about that.”
Arguably the most remarkable part is how Acuña Jr. responded to sitting during a playoff race. Keep in mind the Braves only had a five-game NL East lead over the Phillies when the veteran outfielder rejoined the lineup on Aug. 28. But rather than complain or take things personally, Acuña Jr. took it upon himself to fix what wasn’t working.
Fans and observers can say whatever they want about Acuña Jr., who has frequently drawn pushback for his enthusiasm, celebrations and durability. But he was injured during the Braves’ 2021 title run, and he’s still chasing his first World Series plate appearance. He turns 29 in December and only has two years of team control left; time is running out for him to guarantee himself a nine-figure contract.
But if Acuña Jr. continues to hit how he has of late, the only question is whether he’ll clear $250 million on his next deal. Guiding the Braves to their second championship in six years would go a long way in convincing ownership he’s still worth the risk.

This timing turned a historic stat line into a full-blown vindication for the front office. item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong stole his 40th base on the same afternoon the Chicago Cubs locked up a second straight playoff trip. This timing turned a historic stat line into a full-blown vindication for the front office. The 24-year-old entered the game with 45 homers and 39 steals before taking off against Tyler Phillips in the first inning.
The crowd at Wrigley Field paused to watch him reach second base. One pitch after a leadoff walk, the milestone was official. Only three players in history have hit at least 45 homers while stealing 40 bases in a single season. Crow-Armstrong is now one of them.
The Trade That Changed Everything
Look back at the 2021 trade deadline for the full picture. The Cubs sent Javier Baez and Trevor Williams to the New York Mets. In return, they got Crow-Armstrong, who was just a prospect with recent shoulder surgery. Baez was a hometown hero who helped win the 2016 World Series. Crow-Armstrong had played only six pro games before the deal. His bat was far from a sure thing at the time.
FanSided originally gave the Mets an A- for that swap while the Cubs got a B+. The writers called it a risk then. The Mets could have never imagined such a disastrous outcome for this deal, which has now deteriorated significantly. Crow-Armstrong's 40-40 season proves the Cubs took the right side of the table. They traded a rental player in a lost year for a future MVP.
More Than Just Speed and Power
The numbers go deeper than just the 40-40 club. Earlier this month, his pursuit of high fWAR brought him close to a mark untouched by any National League batter since Bonds. Seiya Suzuki hit the only home run for Chicago in the 2-1 win over the Miami Marlins. The pitching staff protected that narrow lead to seal the victory.
This win guaranteed the Cubs one of the three Wild Card spots in the National League. It marks the first time since 2015 through 2018 that the team reached consecutive postseasons. Crow-Armstrong has secured two All-Star selections and a Gold Glove award already. He signed an extension that keeps him in Chicago through the 2032 campaign.
Compare the results of that 2021 trade. Since the trade, Javier Baez has accumulated 56 homers and 40 stolen bases across 590 games. Crow-Armstrong has 45 homers and 40 steals in less than half that time.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers get A grade in final Post MLB Power Rankings. But who gets an F?

Of course, their repeated failures in recent postseasons mean the real test is still to come in October. They have one superstar in Jacob Misiorowski but will need others to em
item.content:encoded:
Throughout the season, the California Post power-ranked MLB’s 30 teams and checked in on intriguing awards races. Records as of Saturday morning:
1) Brewers (101-59): A+
It was another perfect regular season for the Brewers, who won 100 games for the first time in franchise history to clinch the best record in the majors. Of course, their repeated failures in recent postseasons mean the real test is still to come in October. They have one superstar in Jacob Misiorowski but will need others to emerge in this year’s playoffs.
2) Dodgers (98-62): A
It was a familiar story for the Dodgers this year. A hot start. A second-half slump. Plenty of injuries along the way. Yet, another division crown that sets them up for another deep October run. That formula has worked the past two years for the two-time defending champions. Their real grade this season will depend on whether they can complete a World Series three-peat.
3) Rays (97-63): A+
After two years of missing the playoffs, the Rays had a very Rays-esque season. Uncovered gems on the mound. A relentlessly consistent lineup at the plate. And, as a result, the AL’s best record — and their best chance to get back to the World Series since 2020.
4) Braves (93-67): A
The Braves are back in the playoffs and back atop the NL East, rebounding as hoped from a disappointing 86-loss campaign last season that snapped a six-year postseason streak.
5) Yankees (93-68): B+
This grade might’ve been higher, if not for the uncertainty shrouding the Bronx Bombers as they enter the postseason. They managed to survive one extended Aaron Judge absence this regular season. Trying to do so again in October would be a tall task.
6) Padres (89-71): A-
In the weeks leading up to the trade deadline, the Padres seemed bound to be sellers. But then their offense — especially Fernando Tatis Jr. — came back to life. They bolstered their rotation by being buyers at the trade deadline instead. And now they are back in the playoffs as a potential dark horse, thanks to their 16-5 record in September.
7) Cubs (88-73): B+
The Cubs are back in the playoffs for a second straight year. They have the presumptive National League MVP in Pete Crow-Armstrong. And they managed to overcome a wave of pitching injuries. Now, they will try to mount a deeper October run after being knocked out in Game 5 of the NLDS last year.
8) Red Sox (87-74): B+
A strange regular season in Boston has reached a satisfactory ending, with the Red Sox — led by interim-now-turned-permanent manager Chad Tracy — getting a shot to avenge last year’s postseason elimination to the Yankees in next week’s wild-card series.
9) Phillies (87-73): Incomplete
Check back with us on Sunday night for this final grade. Because after seemingly salvaging their nightmarish start to the season under interim manager Don Mattingly, the Phillies are flirting with what would be a monumental September collapse, having yet to secure their place in the playoffs amid a 2-5 slump this week.
10) Diamondbacks (86-74): B-
We are only tentatively grading the Dbacks for now, thanks to their slim (but very much possible) chances of sneaking into the playoffs. If they don’t, it will be another conflicting season for the Dbacks, who have won 80-plus games in four straight seasons but still have just their surprise 2023 World Series run to show for it.
11) Guardians (84-76): A
The Guardians did what they do this season. Prevent runs. Score just enough. Fly under the radar for most of the year. Then round into form late to (most likely) win another AL Central title.
12) White Sox (83-77): A
This could still become an A+ if the White Sox wind up winning the AL Central. But even if not, the South Siders have been the most pleasant surprise in the majors this season, going from three straight 100-loss seasons to an upstart playoff berth with their young and promising roster.
13/14) Astros/Rangers (79-81): Incomplete
To be clear, neither of these teams has had a good 2026. And yet, they both enter the final days of the season with a chance to win the AL West — even though they can finish no better than .500. It will be the first time in MLB history a team will make the playoffs without a winning record. What a year in the AL West.
15) Pirates (81-79): C+
Good news: The Pirates avoided a losing record for the first time since 2018. Bad news: It wasn’t enough to keep them in playoff contention despite a surprisingly productive year from their offense.
16) Marlins (79-81): C+
The Marlins flirted with playoff contention for a while before ultimately fading down the stretch. They could be poised to take another step next year. Then again, they’ve looked that way before (remember that surprise playoff appearance in 2023?) and been unable to keep progressing.
17) Orioles (79-82): D
The Orioles’ signing of Pete Alonso worked out. But little else did in Baltimore this year. The once-budding contender has now missed the playoffs in two straight years after being swept in back-to-back postseasons the two years before that.
18) Blue Jays (78-82): D
As if the Blue Jays’ post-pennant campaign wasn’t bad enough, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. provided one more low point with his comments about his $500 million contract this week. There is hope for next season. But this year stung.
19) Cardinals (77-83): B
Given nonexistent preseason expectations, the rebuilding Cardinals mostly accomplished what they wanted to this year. They have young talent in Jordan Walker and JJ Wetherholt. They have rebuilt what is now a highly ranked farm system. And they look like a team capable of making a jump in 2027 and beyond.
20) Nationals (76-84): C
The Nats were never serious playoff contenders (their MLB-record 42 blown saves made sure of that). But they have identified a core of young talent to build around. Whether they will spend to add the necessary pieces around them, however, remains to be seen.
21) Mets (73-87): D-
The Mets can only hope this train wreck of a year serves as some sort of cleanse as they look to retool their roster this winter. The only thing that saved this from being an F was their second-half performance under another interim-now-turned-permanent manager in Andy Green.
22) Twins (76-84): C
For some reason, the Twins were intent on being playoff contenders this year. For a while, they hung around in a bad AL wild-card race. But in the end, they’ve wound up back where they started: With an OK, but not-at-all contending, roster that leaves them stuck in MLB’s no-man’s land.
23) Tigers (75-85): D
How much will the Tigers rue their decision to not maximize Tarik Skubal’s trade value by dealing him last winter? It could depend, first and foremost, on River Ryan’s development in their rotation. At the least, he offered signs of promise with a scoreless three-inning debut with the team this week.
24) Reds (74-86): D
Whatever momentum the Reds thought they were building after last year’s postseason berth vanished this summer, despite Elly De La Cruz cementing himself as one of the best players in baseball. The next time their owner asks why they aren’t the Brewers, someone should hold up a mirror.
25) Mariners (74-86): F
At the beginning of the year, only the Dodgers had a higher probability of making the playoffs (according to FanGraphs’ computer models) than the Mariners’ 80.9% mark. Instead, they suffered what might be the most disappointing season in their long-tortured history. They could be good again next year. But this season was a reminder that’s anything but a guarantee.
26) Royals (68-92): D
Another disastrous Royals season leaves them facing an existential crisis, trying to figure out how to return to competitiveness before they waste the prime of Bobby Witt Jr.’s career.
27) Giants (65-95): F
The Giants thought they could be contenders this year. Instead, they now find themselves at a crossroads. They have little choice but to run it back with their thus-far disappointing core of Willy Adames, Matt Chapman and Rafael Devers (plus Logan Webb). But this year, they looked a long way off from even being competitive.
28) Athletics (64-96): D-
There was some thought before the year that the Athletics’ young roster could be feisty. Now, the only question is how much longer they have to waste away in their minor-league ballpark purgatory.
29) Angels (62-98): C
This grade has little to do with the Angels’ on-field product, as they flirt with what would be the first 100-loss season in franchise history, and everything to do with the changes they’ve made behind the scenes. New owner. New front office. And for the first time in a while, new reason for long-term hope.
30) Rockies (57-103): D
The best thing we can say about the Rockies: They proved slightly tougher to beat during this 100-loss season, as opposed to each of the three previous ones they have suffered the last three years. Progress!
Awards Predictions
NL MVP: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
AL MVP: Yordan Alvarez, Astros
NL Cy Young: Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers
AL Cy Young: Cam Schlittler, Yankees
NL Rookie of the Year: Sal Stewart, Reds
AL Rookie of the Year: Kevin McGonigle, Tigers
NL Reliever of the Year: Mason Miller, Padres
AL Reliever of the Year: Louis Varland, Blue Jays

item.content:encoded:
Work with me here.
Imagine that this was Shohei Ohtani’s first MLB season. Thus, this was the first time you regularly saw the same human start 14 games with a 1.79 ERA and produce the fifth-best OPS in the majors.
The attempt is to erase from your mental database familiarity. So you see this fresh and, thus, remove fatigue or boredom or Dodgers hatred or whatever might come when the baseball miraculous is done too often in front of you, rendering it mundane.
If you can attain that state where you see it all anew, let me ask you this: Would you vote for Ohtani as National League MVP?

Baseball Prospectus ranked the Mets’ front office as the 10th best in Major League Baseball.

Kai Chang analyzes the last outing of the year for Zac Thornton.

1986: The Mets defeated the Pirates 3-1 to move to 101-53 on the season. Keith Hernandez drove in two runs, while Sid Fernandez pitched eight strong innings to get the win.

item.title: [New York Post] Shota Imanaga blasts himself in face with beer in wild Cubs celebration
item.dc:creator: Bryan Fonseca
item.description: Shota Imanaga doesn’t need anyone else’s help celebrating. The Cubs pitcher went viral after repeatedly blasting himself in the face with beer during the team’s wild clubhouse celebration after clinching a spot in the postseason Thursday. Naturally, Imanaga had an explanation for the madness. “This is Japanese style,” Imanaga said while holding a bottle in each hand. “Japanese misogi.” Imanaga then turned both bottles toward himself and sprayed the beer directly onto his head and face, bobbing u
item.content:encoded:
Shota Imanaga doesn’t need anyone else’s help celebrating.
The Cubs pitcher went viral after repeatedly blasting himself in the face with beer during the team’s wild clubhouse celebration after clinching a spot in the postseason Thursday.
Naturally, Imanaga had an explanation for the madness.
“This is Japanese style,” Imanaga said while holding a bottle in each hand. “Japanese misogi.”
Imanaga then turned both bottles toward himself and sprayed the beer directly onto his head and face, bobbing up and down into the streams as his teammates laughed around him.
“Self-service!” Imanaga said.
The Cubs leaned into the moment themselves, posting the video on social media captioned: “Who needs bottle service when you have self-service?”
During an interview with Marquee Sports Network’s Taylor McGregor amid the clubhouse celebration, Imanaga was showered with champagne by his teammates.
His response?
“Yummy!”
Chicago officially punched its postseason ticket with a 2-1 victory over the Marlins at Wrigley Field, securing a playoff berth for the second consecutive season.
Seiya Suzuki tied the game with his 26th home run of the season in the fifth inning before Nico Hoerner drove home Ian Happ for the eventual winning run in the sixth.
Pete Crow-Armstrong also stole his 40th base of the season in the victory, giving him 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases and making him just the seventh player in MLB history to accomplish the feat.
Imanaga has played his part in getting Chicago back to the playoffs for the second consecutive season.
The 33-year-old left-hander went 11-10 with a 3.74 ERA while remaining a fixture in Chicago’s starting rotation throughout the season.
He also recorded 171 strikeouts in 173 ⅓ innings pitched in 2026.
Last year, the Cubs went 92-70 and took care of the Padres in the wild-card round before falling to the Brewers in five games in the NLDS.
Imanaga, who was an All-Star two seasons ago, turned 33 earlier this month and has a career 3.44 ERA and a 35-21 record.

item.content:encoded:
Las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) revelaron las 20 camisetas de peloteros más vendidas de la temporada 2026.
En la lista figura un solo pelotero venezolano: Ronald Acuña Jr., de los Bravos de Atlanta, quien ocupa la cuarta posición. En 2025, Acuña Jr. también figuró en este listado, pero en el puesto 11.
La publicación, difundida por la MLB en su cuenta de Instagram, reveló que el japonés Shohei Ohtani, de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, encabeza la lista de las camisetas más vendidas.
En cuanto a los equipos, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles son los que cuentan con más jugadores en la lista, con cuatro: Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts y Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
¿Quiénes son los 20 peloteros con las camisetas más vendidas en 2026?
De acuerdo con la lista difundida por la MLB, estas son las 20 camisetas más vendidas de la temporada 2026:
- Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Aaron Judge, Yankees de Nueva York.
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cachorros de Chicago.
- Ronald Acuña Jr., Bravos de Atlanta.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres de San Diego.
- Freddie Freeman, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Bryce Harper, Filis de Filadelfia.
- Mookie Betts, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Juan Soto, Mets de Nueva York.
- Corey Seager, Texas Rangers.
- Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Toronto Blue Jays.
- Adley Rutschman, Medias Rojas de Boston.
- Kyle Schwarber, Filis de Filadelfia.
- Paul Skenes, Piratas de Pittsburgh.
- Cal Raleigh, Marineros de Seattle.
- Elly De La Cruz, Rojos de Cincinnati.
- Jackson Merrill, Padres de San Diego.
- Nolan Arenado, Arizona Diamondbacks.
- Munetaka Murakami, Chicago White Sox.
Shohei Ohtani encabeza por cuarto año consecutivo
El japonés Shohei Ohtani, de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, volvió a ser el jugador con la camiseta más vendida de las Grandes Ligas, una posición que ocupa por cuarto año consecutivo.
Ohtani se convirtió así en el primer jugador en encadenar cuatro temporadas como líder en ventas de camisetas desde que MLB comenzó a registrar este dato en 2010, reseñó la agencia de noticias EFE este viernes 25 de septiembre.
Desde 2023, los aficionados han comprado la camiseta Nike de Ohtani más que cualquier otra en Estados Unidos, Japón y el resto del mundo, consolidando al jugador japonés como la figura con mayor demanda comercial entre los peloteros de las Grandes Ligas.
El listado, elaborado a partir de las ventas de camisetas Nike realizadas a través de Fanatics, incluido MLBShop.com, desde el Día Inaugural de la temporada 2026, sitúa al capitán de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Judge, en el segundo puesto y al jardinero de los Cachorros de Chicago Pete Crow-Armstrong en el tercero.

item.content:encoded:
El japonés Shohei Ohtani, estrella de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, volvió a ser el jugador con la camiseta más vendida de las Grandes Ligas, una posición que ocupa por cuarto año consecutivo, según la lista publicada este viernes por MLB y MLB Players, Inc. (Mlbpi).
Ohtani se convirtió así en el primer jugador desde que MLB comenzó a registrar las ventas en 2010, que encadena cuatro temporadas como líder en comercialización de camisetas.
Desde 2023, los aficionados han comprado la camiseta Nike de Ohtani más que cualquier otra en Estados Unidos, Japón y el resto del mundo, consolidando al jugador japonés como la figura con mayor demanda comercial entre los peloteros de las Grandes Ligas.
El listado, elaborado a partir de las ventas de camisetas Nike realizadas a través de Fanatics, incluido MLBShop.com, desde el Día Inaugural de la temporada 2026, sitúa al capitán de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Judge, en el segundo puesto y al jardinero de los Cachorros de Chicago Pete Crow-Armstrong en el tercero.
Crow-Armstrong, quien esta temporada se convirtió en el séptimo jugador en la historia de las Mayores y el primero de los Cachorros en conectar al menos 40 jonrones y robar 40 bases, alcanzó el mejor puesto para un jugador de Chicago desde que el puertorriqueño Javier Báez fue tercero en 2018.
El listado también refleja la presencia de otras figuras de alcance internacional. El venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr., de los Bravos de Atlanta, ocupa el cuarto lugar, seguido por el dominicano Fernando Tatis Jr., de los Padres de San Diego.
Los Dodgers colocaron a tres jugadores entre los diez primeros, con Ohtani al frente, Freddie Freeman en el sexto puesto y Mookie Betts en el octavo. El japonés Yoshinobu Yamamoto, también de Los Ángeles, aparece noveno.
La temporada 2026 marcó además un registro inédito para los jugadores japoneses, con tres de ellos entre los 20 primeros de la clasificación, después de que el toletero Munetaka Murakami, de los Medias Blancas de Chicago, debutara en el vigésimo puesto.
Yamamoto, por su parte, ocupa el noveno lugar, mientras que Ohtani mantiene el liderazgo de una clasificación que vuelve a poner de manifiesto su dimensión dentro y fuera del terreno de juego.
La lista se conoce antes del inicio de las Series de Comodines de ambas ligas, que comenzarán el próximo martes 29 de septiembre, con Ohtani, Judge y Crow-Armstrong entre las principales figuras de unos equipos que ya tienen asegurado su boleto a la Postemporada.

item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed

item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong is the favorite to win the National League MVP Award, and even his rivals have nothing but great things to say about him.
The Cubs once again fell short of winning the National League Central, watching the Brewers' four-peat for the first time in the division's history. The Brewers have their own MVP Award winner in Christian Yelich. Yelich won MVP in 2018 and was the favorite to win a second MVP Award in 2019 before a knee injury in the final month of the regular season.
It's been a while since Yelich won MVP, but at his peak he was a dynamic power-speed threat, just like Crow-Armstrong. Yelich didn't have the advantage that Crow-Armstrong does on the bases with all of the new rules, but he was still able to make a difference at the plate with his power and with his legs on the basepaths. Yelich acknowledged how good a hitter Crow-Armstrong has been this year, despite playing for his rival team.
"He's probably the best defender in the game right now, and it'd be hard to find another hitter that's going as good as he is," Yelich said, per ESPN's Jesse Rogers. "He's had a great year and a special year for him."
Yelich's MVP season was great, but it did not feature Platinum Glove defense.
"Yes, without the defense," Yelich said when asked if he sees similarities between his MVP season and Crow-Armstrong's. "That's what makes him really, really special -- is being able to combine the two."
Crow-Armstrong should win the Platinum Glove this year, and there's a good chance his Cubs and Yelich's Brewers meet in the postseason.
More MLB: Cubs' Jed Hoyer Has Unbelievably High Praise For Pete Crow-Armstrong's Season

item.title: [MLB.com] Bregman back in Cubs lineup just days after being hit in face with foul ball
item.dc:creator: Jordan Bastian

item.content:encoded:
BOSTON – No one really knew what the road back to the field would look like for Alex Bregman in the immediate aftermath of the scary scene on Sunday in Cincinnati. The Cubs’ star third baseman was struck in the left side of the face by a foul ball and sustained multiple fractures, making his well-being the biggest concern.
On Friday morning at Fenway Park, Bregman’s name was back in the lineup for the Cubs, who slotted the veteran in as the designated hitter in the lineup’s third spot. Given the initial shock of his injury, having Bregman back so soon came not only as a relief, but as a potential boost as Chicago nears a National League Wild Card Series.
“It’s incredible,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said.
The Cubs understand there is risk involved with having Bregman return to the lineup less than a week removed from the incident, but the third baseman went through multiple days of workouts and was cleared by the team’s doctors. After Bregman showed no concussion symptoms, passed vision testing and was deemed not to require surgery, Friday was circled as a possible target for his comeback.
Bregman began with tracking pitches against the high-velocity Trajekt machine at Wrigley Field on Tuesday and advanced to hitting on Wednesday. By Thursday, the third baseman was out in the field going through running drills to test how that felt. And as the Cubs celebrated their postseason clinch on Thursday night, Bregman stayed to the side at his locker, protected from the fray by plastic sheeting hanging in the locker room.
Counsell noted that Bregman was “itching to get in” Thursday’s clincher against the Marlins.
“There were a lot of unknowns,” Counsell said. “It was a freak injury. It’s an injury that we don’t deal with very often, that you don’t experience very often, so you’re kind of unaware of the risk and things like that. There are risks. And we’ve talked to Alex about that, but I think we’ve done the best we can to minimize them and just move forward.”
Bregman was waiting on deck at Great American Ball Park on Sunday, when Michael Busch checked his swing and fouled off a pitch from Reds pitcher Luis Mey in the fourth inning. Bregman had little time to react and immediately grabbed at his face and headed down the tunnel before being taken to a local hospital.
A staffer remained in Cincinnati to drive Bregman back to Chicago and the third baseman posted a photo on Instagram of his bruised, bloodied face with his left eye swollen shut. The swelling reduced significantly in the days leading up to the trip to Boston and Bregman planned on wearing a modified helmet to help guard against any setbacks.
In that social media post, Bregman declared, “I’ll be back,” and he delivered faster on that promise than fans might have expected.
Counsell said Bregman’s personality and drive to stay on the field have made an impact on the Cubs this season.
“Look, Alex’s best trait is just, the man loves baseball,” Counsell said. “And he’s super competitive. And he’s relentless in his pursuit to be a little bit better. And so, that just rubs off on people. And he talks about it non-stop. I mean, every one of us has gotten late-night texts or observations, so it’s great.
“And it makes you love it, and it makes you want to go to battle with him.”
While Pete Crow-Armstrong has emerged as the NL’s favorite to take home the MVP Award, Bregman has also turned in the type of season that should get down-ballot consideration. Through 153 games, Bregman had 5.2 fWAR with 26 homers, 32 doubles, 89 RBIs and an .804 OPS to go along with Gold Glove-caliber defense. He has really taken off since the All-Star break, posting a .978 OPS.
And with his return to the lineup, Bregman is on the cusp of playing in the postseason for a 10th consecutive season.
“His relentlessness is infectious,” Counsell said.

Around the league…
- With their win over the Royals yesterday, the White Sox clinched their ticket to the postseason. However, you will not see Luis Castillo on the playoff roster since he was placed on the injured list with a shoulder injury.
- This is not surprising but good confirmation to have.
- In recent years, it's been extremely rare for a player who qualifies for the batting average title to go homerless in a season. Yet, the Rays' Chandler Simpson is on track to do just that, writes Davy Andrews at Fangraphs.
- Yes, pitchers really are throwing harder than they ever have before.
- We need more Joey Vottos on television.
"The guy that used to hit .300, I'm sorry to tell you, is going to hit .240, .250 today. It just is what it is."@JoeyVotto breaks down why the league does not have more players like Luis Arraez and explains how baseball's evolution has led to that trend. pic.twitter.com/3C5fEUsv1s

item.content:encoded:
It should be a fun weekend in terms of which player wins the MLB home run crown, but I'll be happy either way because it will be either former Cub Kyle Schwarber or current Cubbies superstar and NL MVP lock Pete Crow-Armstrong as they are tied for the overall lead with 45 dingers apiece. I'd actually be fine with a tie. And both should play most of the weekend because their respective teams are playing for better NL wild card seeding. Not sure I see an advantage with both priced -110 to win it.
Those who want to get into , particularly home run prop betting, need to take a look at what I'm playing for Friday's games. Over the past four MLB seasons, I'm up $1,681 on MLB picks. You can find more of my picks at SportsLine, and in the member-exclusive SportsLine Discord server, a community of sports betting enthusiasts and SportsLine experts.
Last Friday, my home run picks were the Diamondbacks' Nolan Arenado at +630 vs. the Yankees as well as the Braves' Mike Yastrzemski +630 against the Astros. Arenado didn't homer but had two hits so I cashed Over 1.5 total bases -- all my home run prop picks mean I like Over 1.5 total bases even better at the . Yaz, meanwhile, was 0-for-4 with two strikeouts. Bummer.
Top MLB home run picks for Friday, Sept. 25
- Pete Alonso, Orioles (+394, DrafKings)
- Drake Baldwin, Braves (+360, FanDuel)
Pete Alonso, Orioles (+394, DraftKings)
This three-game AL East series between Baltimore and New York from Yankee Stadium that begins tonight at 7:05 ET is meaningless in the grand scheme of things. The Bombers are locked into the AL's top wild card spot and the Orioles are eliminated and can't even finish with a winning record. So long story short, I won't be betting a side here. WT.
I personally won't be touching any playoff-bound stars this weekend in terms of props because they might sit out or be pulled midway through a game to rest up and be as healthy as possible for the postseason, which starts Tuesday. And we've already been told by the Yankees that Aaron Judge will not be back from his latest injury for the Wild Card Series. That's a bummer. Although he claims he will play. We shall see.
But certainly there are players out there who have individual goals they want to meet by Sunday either for personal reasons or a financial incentive via bonus. Pete Alonso was Baltimore's big-ticket free-agent addition, and Alonso struggled early on as many stars do when leaving a team for the first time in free agency. But Alonso has been raking for weeks and could win the AL home run title. He currently has 41 and is in a four-way tie for first.
Alonso has become the first Orioles player since Anthony Santander in 2024 to get to 40 dingers, and Alonso already has easily cashed Over his spring total of 37.5. He was named the team MVP this week, the first unanimous Most Valuable Oriole since outfielder Cedric Mullins in 2021. While Alonso is a righty masher, he has a lot better numbers against right-handed pitchers and faces one tonight in New York's Will Warren (10-6, 4.02 ERA), who has given up 20 homers on the year. Alonso is 2-for-7 off him with two solo homers. I can't really recommend any other Orioles batters.
Drake Baldwin, Braves (+360, FanDuel)
An NL East series between Atlanta and Miami starts at 7:05 ET from South Florida, and I'm guessing there will be plenty of good seats available on a beautiful Florida fall night with high school football going strong. No weather concerns as the retractable roof at loanDepot Park is usually closed. They all are usually closed.
There is nothing at stake here, so I'm hoping the Braves include Drake Baldwin in the lineup. They are the NL East champions and will host the last NL wild card team in that round next week. I hope that's Philadelphia just for rivalry purposes. About the only carrot for the Marlins is to finish at .500.
If Miami can find some hitting in the offseason, it could be pretty decent in 2027 (if there is a season) because the Marlins have some good starting pitching led by fire-balling righty Eury Perez (7-11, 4.14 ERA), who goes tonight. Perez made his first career relief appearance on Tuesday at the Cubs in a 12-inning game but that will basically serve as his off-day bullpen session having thrown just one inning. Perez has surrendered 20 homers on the year.
With Seattle's Cal Raleigh falling way off this year, you could argue that lefty-hitting Drake Baldwin of the Braves is the best all-around offensive catcher in MLB -- although he plays at DH plenty. Baldwin has 24 homers and a slugging percentage of .456. Baldwin's power has disappeared a bit in September with only two homers, but he's 4-for-9 off Perez with two homers.

item.title: [North Side Baseball] 'Listen to This Crowd': Pete Crow-Armstrong's Capstone Moment Epitomized One of Chicago Sports' Greatest Seasons
item.dc:creator: Matthew Trueblood
item.description: Cubs Video If the Wrigley Field crowd had had its way, the game might have stopped for a while. Speeches could have been given. The commissioner could have strode onto the field, while a microphone was hastily placed behind home plate. A ceremony could have been performed. Certainly, a long video of highlights and tributes would have met no great resistance. Pete Crow-Armstrong, however, just tried to keep it together. "Don't cry on the baseball field—not that that's not ok," Crow-Armstrong said
item.content:encoded:
Cubs Video
If the Wrigley Field crowd had had its way, the game might have stopped for a while. Speeches could have been given. The commissioner could have strode onto the field, while a microphone was hastily placed behind home plate. A ceremony could have been performed. Certainly, a long video of highlights and tributes would have met no great resistance. Pete Crow-Armstrong, however, just tried to keep it together.
"Don't cry on the baseball field—not that that's not ok," Crow-Armstrong said after the game, when asked what was going through his mind at second base, "but that's emotional stuff. I mean, I've gotten so much love, and I'm so lucky for that, and it's something I'm grateful for every day."
Crow-Armstrong had just stolen his 40th base of the season, putting him in the illustrious 40/40 club. It was the chance the fans needed to finally hit him with the waves of adulation that had been lapping at the shore for weeks—to crash over him with their admiration and gratitude for what has been the greatest individual season in Cubs history.
There's something a bit tawdry and small, really, about 40/40. Power and speed in the same package was once quite rare, and indeed, speed was not applied on the field the way it is now until roughly the mid-1950s. Now, though, the best athletes on the diamond are often capable of both hitting for power and stealing bases. José Canseco opened the 40/40 club in 1988, generating a certain amount of awe, but (while relatively few players have followed him through the door he busted open) power-speed combos are much more common now.
Statistically, the club evokes a blend of thunder and lightning, but it sketches them roughly. The two achievements are monumentally imbalanced. Every home run is worth about four times as much as a stolen base. Counting up these two particular events is also a bit unsatisfying, unless you grew up with the numbers on the back of an old-fashioned baseball card. Doubles and triples matter; walks matter; taking extra bases on non-steals matter. When you hear that someone has accomplished 40/40, there's a suggestion of well-roundedness that extends beyond power and speed, but that suggestion has often been deception. Canseco was a meathead who played like one, hurting his team with poor defense and bad baserunning decisions. Alfonso Soriano drew so few walks that power was almost his whole game offensively, and he, too, was a lousy defender.
Still, it was an occasion. It was like a birthday party, when we half-arbitrarily find an excuse to celebrate someone for no real reason other than that we love and are thankful for them. Crow-Armstrong's achievement, if it had only been 40 homers and 40 steals, would have meant something, but not something huge. The season he's had, though, merited something more than applause in response to each individual moment of mastery. He's been much too heroic not to stop and marvel.
The full 40/40 club is, as you've heard a dozen times by now, Canseco, Alfonso Soriano, Barry Bonds, Álex Rodríguez, Ronald Acuña Jr., Shohei Ohtani, and Crow-Armstrong. That company is illustrious, but we can do even better. According to Baseball Reference, Crow-Armstrong is also a member of the 40/15/10 club: 40 or more runs above average at the plate; 15 or more runs above average as a fielder; and 10 or more runs above average via baserunning and double-play avoidance. That club has only two other members: Rickey Henderson, in 1980, and Mike Trout, in 2012.
If you want to confine yourself to stats based on raw outcomes without adjustments or interpretations, we can still do better than merely counting homers and steals. Crow-Armstrong has 355 total bases and has drawn 82 walks. The only players with 350 or more total bases, 75 or more walks and 30 or more steals in a season are Crow-Armstrong, Ohtani, Acuña, Vladimir Guerrero, Larry Walker, Henry Aaron and Willie Mays. The only 40/40 club members who were caught stealing fewer than 10 times the year they achieved their status were Bonds and Ohtani; Crow-Armstrong has only been caught seven times.
It's important that we link Crow-Armstrong's season to these names—Mays, Bonds, Trout and Ohtani, especially. That conveys how great his campaign has been in an honest way. We have another 10 years to find out whether he can actually be as good as those guys, but this year has been as good as those guys' best. That, in itself, is remarkable. However, it's not what the fans were really cheering for. Rather, what has made Crow-Armstrong's summer so special is all the resonances that supersede the national attention and the historic accolades for Chicagoans: the ones that tie him inextricably to this city and its pride in its sports history.
Obviously, no Cubs player had ever before gone 40/40, but just as importantly, only one player in the annals of the franchise had ever stolen 40 and hit 40 homers in any season, even if it be two separate ones: Ryne Sandberg, whose death (too young) last July is still a visible scar on the hearts of Cubs fans. Billy Williams (happily, still with us) was the only left-handed hitter ever to hit 40 homers in a season for the team. Crow-Armstrong's baserunning regularly elicits comparisons to Javier Báez. His sonic boom of a gear shift in late May and throughout June evoked Sammy Sosa, who later showed up for the team's celebration of its 150th anniversary and prophesized about the three-homer game Crow-Armstrong produced that very day.
Crow-Armstrong has knitted himself into the fabric of the franchise by weaving his own legacy as warp across the weft of the team's greatest and most beloved stars. It hasn't all happened this year, but it all came together this year. He filled a hole, too. A team that has had a franchise shortstop (Ernie Banks), a franchise second baseman (Sandberg), a franchise third baseman (Ron Santo), a franchise first baseman (Mark Grace, Anthony Rizzo, take your pick), a franchise left fielder (Williams) and a franchise right fielder (Sosa) has never had a truly great center fielder. That has finally changed.
In the same way he seems to be stretching across and enmeshing himself within team history, he's doing the same with the wider Chicago sports landscape. His friendship with Caleb Williams has been exhaustively documented, but when Williams, Matas Buzelis, Caleb Wilson and more showed up to sit in the front row behind the Cubs dugout one night late in the summer, the point was driven home. Crow-Armstrong is part of a wave of talent that gives an underachieving sports town new hope for shaking off that label.
Of course, when you talk about Chicago sports icons, there's really only one name. That one didn't come into direct contact with Crow-Armstrong's this year, and maybe it never will. The comparisons are going to become unavoidable soon enough, though. Crow-Armstrong isn't the next Sosa, or the next Báez, or the next Sandberg. He's not just Caleb Williams or Conor Bedard. Though he comes in (so far, anyway) a much more grounded, cuddly outer wrapping, Crow-Armstrong is a hurricane of talent and ambition as strong as Michael Jordan—the only athlete about whom that can be said who has stepped foot in the city since Jordan left it.
That's what fans respond to so forcefully, even if most of them don't realize it. They're not explicitly looking to recapitulate the 1990s Bulls, because we do not live our lives solely in reference to our pasts, but then again, our pasts are never really past, are they? They don't actively want another Jordan, whose toxicity toward teammates would never fly now and was irresponsible even then. They don't expect six championships from Crow-Armstrong, because that would be utterly unreasonable; it's not how baseball works, or how the 21st century works.
But that's what Crow-Armstrong is. What fans love is not only his talent, but the drive they can see on his face, and the way he seems to sizzle with the need to win. He's not without swagger, but while outsiders might misconstrue his attitude as selfish or self-aggrandizing, Cubs fans know better. What they see—what objective viewers can see, too, as long as they don't bring too much of their own baggage to the viewing party—is that Crow-Armstrong's every move and thought is oriented toward winning. He argues vehemently with umpires, but only on behalf of his team—never when the stakes are only his own statistics. He hustles unreservedly. He slams his bat and fires his helmet when things are going badly, but it's all born of the eagerness he feels to deliver on the fans' demands or to save his shaky team from itself.
He doesn't, for instance, rack up garbage-time steals. Of his 40 thefts this year, only nine came in low-leverage situations; that's 22.5%. In the modern game (especially since the rules changes that bolstered the running game in 2023), the percentage of steals that come in unimportant moments has risen.
Crow-Armstrong, though, has just those nine steals and has only been caught once when it didn't matter much. Even most of the technically low-leverage steals came as the back half of a first-and-third play, or in the third inning, when things were far from decided. He's no stat padder, and yet, look how good his stats are.
The Cubs will win a World Series with Crow-Armstrong, someday. It probably won't be this year, but it will happen. That that feels so certain is not just a reflection of his talent, the way a Bears fan might say that Williams's talent at a position with so much power makes an eventual Super Bowl win feel likely. It's more. It's the way Crow-Armstrong carries himself. It's the maturity it has taken for him to handle his exploding fame relatively well, and to listen to teammates and get better because of his interactions with them. It's the sagacity of his thoughts on the game itself—on his craft. He's as detail-oriented and hard-working as Jordan, but a better teammate. He's a winner.
He's also, of course, going to be here a while. That's the final thing that went through the crowd, as they applauded so long and loud in that moment after Crow-Armstrong's landmark steal. As warm as the memories of the 2016 team will always be for most fans, those players all left. The only ones to sign contract extensions after joining the organization were Rizzo and Kyle Hendricks. The only one to sign a long-term deal after the title itself was Hendricks. It's easier for players to move on, these days, and if many fans couldn't imagine Kris Bryant ever wearing another uniform after he was the centerpiece of that championship drought-breaking team, they're wiser and sadder now.
Crow-Armstrong is the cure for that sadness, without dimming the wisdom. He's extremely proud to be a Cub. He's going to be a Cub for a long time. And he's finishing the greatest season ever put together by a Cub. His willingness to belong to the team and the city has made the city desperate to show him how much they also feel they belong to him. Sports or not, in 2026, it's even harder to find that kind of mutual devotion than it is to find 40 homers and 40 steals on one baseball card.

item.title: [fieldlevelmedia.com] Pete Crow-Armstrong joins 40/40 club as Cubs clinch wild-card spot
item.description: Pete Crow-Armstrong became the seventh player in MLB history with a 40-40 season, as he stole his 40th base of the season Thursday, the same day his Chicago Cubs clinched a playoff berth. Crow-Armstrong, who is tied for the MLB lead with 45 home runs, joins Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to collect at least 40 homers and 40 steals in a season. The favorite for National Le
item.content:encoded:
Pete Crow-Armstrong became the seventh player in MLB history with a 40-40 season, as he stole his 40th base of the season Thursday, the same day his Chicago Cubs clinched a playoff berth.
Crow-Armstrong, who is tied for the MLB lead with 45 home runs, joins Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to collect at least 40 homers and 40 steals in a season.
The favorite for National League Most Valuable Player walked to lead off the first inning against the visiting Miami Marlins and promptly stole second base.
He was stranded at third that inning, but the Cubs (88-71) went on to beat the Marlins 2-1 to lock in their NL wild-card playoff spot with three games to go.
Crow-Armstrong, 24, has played in all 159 games for the Cubs this season and batted .280 with 107 RBIs. His 45 long balls are tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

25 Sep 2026, 02:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Matt Marton)
Nico Hoerner ripped a go-ahead RBI single in the sixth and Matthew Boyd tossed seven strong innings, helping the host Chicago Cubs clinch a playoff berth with a 2-1 victory over the Miami Marlins on Thursday afternoon.
Chicago's Pete Crow-Armstrong walked to lead off the first inning and promptly stole second base to become the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases in a single season. Armstrong, who has 45 homers, joined Jose Canseco (1988), Barry Bonds (1996), Alex Rodriguez (1998), Alfonso Soriano (2006), Ronald Acuna Jr. (2023) and Shohei Ohtani (2024) as the only players to reach the 40-40 milestone.
Seiya Suzuki belted a solo homer in the fifth inning to highlight his two-hit performance for the Cubs (88-71), who salvaged the finale of their three-game series with Miami.
Boyd (10-5) allowed one run on five hits to record his second straight victory following a 0-4 stretch over his previous six starts.
Daniel Palencia bridged the gap to Ryan Zeferjahn, who retired the side in order in the ninth inning to secure his seventh save of the season.
Jakob Marsee had an RBI single in the third inning for the Marlins (78-81), who have lost four of their last six games.
With the game tied 1-1, Ian Happ tripled off Jack Ralston (0-2) to lead off the sixth inning and came home on Hoerner's RBI single to left field.
Ralston permitted two runs on three hits in 1 1/3 innings.
Brian Navarreto doubled to lead off the third inning against Matthew Boyd before coming home on Marsee's RBI single to center to open the scoring.
Suzuki forged a tie in the fifth inning, depositing a 1-0 pitch from Ralston over the wall in center field. The homer was Suzuki's 26th of the season and second in his last four games.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Alex Bregman's wild MLB playoff streak has star in rare air – injured face willing
Major League Baseball’s playoffs are coming soon and Alex Bregman will be a part of it.
Of course he is.
Bregman made baseball history Thursday, Sept. 24 when the Chicago Cubs clinched a National League wild-card berth with a victory over the Miami Marlins. And for the 10th consecutive year, injured eye willing, Bregman will take part in the postseason, this time with a twist.
Bregman, the Cubs’ 32-year-old third baseman, will become the first position player to play postseason baseball 10 consecutive seasons with multiple teams. In fact, he’s done it with three ballclubs – eight straight years with the Houston Astros and then the past two with the Boston Red Sox and Cubs, as he settled for good in Chicago by signing a five-year, $175 million contract in January.
And it seems like wherever Bregman goes, October baseball follows.
Texas loves him anyway
Bregman was a two-time All-Star and two-time champion in Houston, the brash young slugger in his first full season when they won the 2017 World Series, the MVP runner-up when they lost the 2019 Series in seven games.
After bearing much of the scorn for the club’s 2017 sign-stealing scandal, he was the chastened veteran on the 2022 squad that won a second World Series, this time without a cloud of controversy to follow.
Yet Bregman’s chops as a club cornerstone gained greater veracity a year ago, when he left the Astros and, combining his production with his baseball smarts and clubhouse gravitas, lifted the Red Sox to the postseason for the first time in three years as the Astros missed the playoffs for the first time since 2016.
Those vibes were as attractive to the Cubs as Bregman’s career .846 OPS when they pursued him after he opted out of his contract with Boston. And it’s all come together in Wrigleyville: Thanks to a second-half surge, Bregman has hit 26 home runs, posted an .804 OPS and produced 5.4 WAR, second only to presumed MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong on the Cubs.
“Anytime Alex Bregman is playing an Alex Bregman brand of baseball, it’s just good for the program,” Crow-Armstrong told USA TODAY Sports last month.
And if he manages to play just days after suffering a gruesome eye injury, the legend will only grow.
Heroes of the fall
Bregman’s postseason constancy has put himself among some legendary and curious October stalwarts.
Unsurprisingly, the consecutive postseasons list is littered with alumni from the three dominant playoff groups of the wild-card era: The 1990s Atlanta Braves, the late-century New York Yankees and the current batch of Los Angeles Dodgers.
Yankees closer Mariano Rivera tops the list, appearing in 13 consecutive postseasons from 1995-2007, followed by Derek Jeter, whose 12-year streak began a year after Rivera’s playoff debut.
Catcher Jorge Posada and Braves Hall of Famers Chipper Jones and Tom Glavine all played in 11 consecutive postseasons. As did lefty reliever Mike Stanton, who did it with four teams – the Braves, Red Sox, Yankees and Texas Rangers – between 1991-2002.
Who let him in?
Bregman, longtime Dodgers closer Kenley Jansen and Hall of Famer Greg Maddux all reached 10 consecutive postseasons. Current Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman and longtime third baseman Justin Turner are at the nine-year mark, Freddie winning a World Series championship with Atlanta in 2021 and two more in L.A. the past two seasons.
Retired Dodgers lefty Clayton Kershaw leads the “but for” category: He pitched in eight consecutive postseasons from 2013-2020, and would have made it 13 in a row if not for injuries in 2021 and 2024. Same with Braves Hall of Famer John Smoltz – he was present for all of Atlanta’s 14 consecutive division titles yet underwent Tommy John surgery in 2000.
And several likely 2026 participants had streaks broken thanks to one unlucky season – such as slugger Kyle Schwarber, who’d be working on a 12-year streak with the Cubs, Red Sox and Phillies if not for the 2019 Cubs missing the playoffs. Same with Mookie Betts, ticketed for his 10th postseason in 11 years with the Dodgers and Boston, missing only in ’19 with the Red Sox.
The wild-card format – which began in 1995 and expanded in 2012 and 2022 – makes this list unavoidably modern due to the expanded access it affords. Still, some players from past eras were near-constants in the playoffs.
Mr. October himself, Reggie Jackson, reached the postseason 10 times in 12 years from 1971 to 1982, winning four World Series with the Oakland Athletics and New York Yankees, and then, just for kicks, reaching the 1982 ALCS with the California Angels.
The great Yogi Berra was a 10-time World Series champion, but his longest consecutive streak of playoff runs was five years. Yet reaching the World Series 14 times in 17 years, when only two teams reached the playoffs, remains a stunning feat.
So perhaps Bregman - even with 102 career postseason games, 19 homers, 91 hits and a .791 OPS - has a little more work to do to match some of the legends of October. Yet from Houston to Boston to Chicago, he’s leaving little doubt that wherever he goes, winning follows.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Chandler Simpson Is the Homerless Qualifier We’ve Been Waiting For
item.dc:creator: Davy Andrews
